records.statement: BIS Working Paper No 1194 of June 2024, by Iñaki Aldasoro, Leonardo Gambacorta, Anton Korinek, Vatsala Shreeti and Merlin Stein, states that machine learning models have compounded the risks of uniformity and model herding, and that correlated autonomous actions by AI agents could produce correlated failures in finance.
records.qualification: A staff working paper, attributed to its authors under the series disclaimer, not a BIS position. It states a risk; it does not report that AI-driven herding has been observed.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 5, introduction
evidence.passage: With machine learning models, the risks of uniformity, model herding and network connectedness have only compounded.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 16, section on financial stability
evidence.passage: Correlated failures, in the form of flash crashes due to correlated autonomous actions might happen in a different form in financial intermediation, asset management, insurance and payments.

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2024 (chapter III) states that the behaviour of financial institutions using the same algorithms could amplify procyclicality and market volatility by exacerbating herding, liquidity hoarding, runs and fire sales.

time.note: Chapter released 25 June 2024 according to the BIS press release.

records.qualification: It states a possible risk; it does not report observed herding.

evidence.locator: Section 'Financial system impact of AI', paragraph beginning 'The reliance of market participants on the same handful of algorithms'
evidence.passage: The behaviour of financial institutions using the same algorithms could amplify procyclicality and market volatility by exacerbating herding, liquidity hoarding, runs and fire sales.

records.statement: FSI Insights No 63 of December 2024, by Juan Carlos Crisanto, Cris Benson Leuterio, Jermy Prenio and Jeffery Yong, lists herding behaviour among the macroprudential risks of AI, describing it as the amplification of procyclical behaviour through the use of similar data sets and AI models by multiple financial institutions.
records.qualification: A staff paper under the FSI series disclaimer. The passage is one entry of a table of risk types; the paper does not report that the risk has materialised.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 13 (printed p. 10), Table 4, row 'Herding behaviour'
evidence.passage: Amplification of procyclical behaviour due to the use of similar data sets and AI models by multiple financial institutions

records.statement: In remarks prepared for delivery on 20 October 2026, Tao Zhang, BIS Chief Representative for Asia and the Pacific, said that financial institutions using similar models, data or decision rules may take similar actions at the same time, and that such correlated responses could amplify price movements.
records.qualification: The speaker's own views under his disclaimer, not a BIS position. The remarks describe a potential channel, not an observed episode.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Common expectations can support investment and innovation'
evidence.passage: Financial institutions may use similar models, data or decision rules in trading, lending and risk management. If those tools lead them to interpret information similarly, they may take similar actions at the same time, creating crowded trades or synchronised changes in lending and risk appetite.

records.statement: In a keynote speech of 17 April 2024, Pablo Hernández de Cos, then Chair of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and Governor of the Bank of Spain, said that AI/ML models have yet to be seen across a full financial cycle and could, left unchecked, potentially amplify future banking crises.
records.missing: The retrieved passage names no mechanism of similar models, data or techniques making firms' decisions alike; only the opening of the speech was retrieved, and the full text may say more.
records.qualification: The speaker's own views under his disclaimer. Recorded from the opening paragraphs published on the BIS page only.

evidence.locator: BIS page, paragraph beginning 'My main message is'
evidence.passage: Left unchecked, such models could potentially amplify future banking crises.

records.statement: The Basel Committee's newsletter of 16 March 2022 on AI and machine learning states that its continuing discussions will cover the potential implications of broader usage of AI/ML models for the resilience of individual banks and for financial stability.
records.missing: Names financial stability as an area for analysis but states no mechanism of correlated or herding behaviour.
records.qualification: The newsletter states it is for information only and is not supervisory guidance.

evidence.locator: Third of the three areas listed for continuing discussions
evidence.passage: The third area named for continuing discussions is the potential implications of broader usage of AI/ML models for the resilience of individual banks and, more broadly, for financial stability.

records.statement: The Basel Committee's report 'Digitalisation of finance' of May 2024 states that concentration risks may arise from foundation AI models and from third parties such as cloud service providers and AI model developers, and that broad adoption of generative AI may lead to greater third-party concentration risks.
records.qualification: A Basel Committee report describing possible risks; it does not report that a provider failure has occurred or set new requirements.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 25 (printed p. 21), section 4, bullet 'Concentration risks'
evidence.passage: concentration risks may arise in the form of market infrastructure (eg the Ethereum blockchain), models (eg foundation AI models) or third parties (eg cloud service providers and AI model developers).

evidence.locator: PDF p. 26 (printed p. 22), Box 8 'Generative AI risks', closing paragraph
evidence.passage: greater third-party concentration risks, particularly where the model vendors are also providing cloud services to banks.

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2024 (chapter III) states that relying on a few providers of AI models increases third-party dependency risks, and that any failure of or cyber attack on these providers poses risks to the financial institutions relying on them.
records.qualification: States a risk arising from market structure; it reports no provider failure.

evidence.locator: Section 'Financial system impact of AI', paragraph beginning 'Another operational risk arises'
evidence.passage: Another operational risk arises from relying on just a few providers of AI models, which increases third-party dependency risks.

evidence.locator: Same paragraph, last sentence
evidence.passage: Any failure among or cyber attack on these providers, or their models, poses risks to financial institutions relying on them.

records.statement: FSI Insights No 63 of December 2024, by Crisanto, Leuterio, Prenio and Yong, states that the concentration of cloud and AI service providers in a few large global technology firms strengthens the argument for direct oversight frameworks for these providers.
records.qualification: A staff paper under the FSI series disclaimer; it notes that the prevalent approach still relies on financial institutions managing third-party risks.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 2), executive summary, bullet 'Regulatory perimeter – third parties'
evidence.passage: The concentration of cloud and AI service providers to a few large global technology firms strengthens the argument for putting in place direct oversight frameworks for these service providers depending on available legal authority.

records.statement: The Basel Committee's newsletter of 16 March 2022 on AI and machine learning states that AI/ML deployment, through large data sets, interconnectivity with third parties and cloud use, can create multiple possible points of cyber risk.
records.qualification: The newsletter states it is for information only and is not supervisory guidance; the passage concerns operational and cyber risk in banks, not fraud against customers.

evidence.locator: Second paragraph of the main text, beginning 'In its discussions to date'
evidence.passage: As AI/ML deployment often involves the use of large data sets, interconnectivity with third parties, and the use of cloud technologies, it can also create multiple possible points of cyber risk.

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2024 (chapter III) states that generative AI could vastly expand hackers' ability to write phishing emails and malware, exposing financial institutions and their customers to a greater risk of fraud, and that prompt injection and data or model poisoning add new sources of cyber risk.
records.qualification: States risks; the same chapter also reports that central bank cyber experts surveyed by the BIS deem gen AI to offer more benefits than risks for cyber security.

evidence.locator: Section 'Financial system impact of AI', paragraph beginning 'The reliance on AI heightens concerns about cyber attacks'
evidence.passage: Gen AI could vastly expand hackers' ability to write credible phishing emails or to write malware and use it to steal valuable information or encrypt a company's files for ransom.

evidence.locator: Same paragraph, last sentence
evidence.passage: These developments expose financial institutions and their customers to a greater risk of fraud.

records.statement: The Basel Committee's report 'Digitalisation of finance' of May 2024 states that fraudsters can use deepfakes, synthetic media generated with AI, to commit account takeovers, loan fraud or wire fraud against bank customers.
records.qualification: Describes a fraud risk among the risks of digitalisation; it gives no measure of incidence.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 23 (printed p. 19), section 4, bullet 'Fraud-related risks'
evidence.passage: This can include, for example, the use of deepfakes (a type of synthetic media technology that uses AI to manipulate or generate visual and audio content that appears real) to commit account takeovers, loan fraud or wire fraud.

records.statement: FSI Insights No 35 of August 2021, by Jermy Prenio and Jeffery Yong, states that humans can be held unambiguously accountable for human-based modelling, and that accountability for AI is complicated by, among other factors, the lack of model explainability.
records.qualification: A staff paper under the FSI series disclaimer; it frames explainability as one of three compounding factors in a challenge of accountability.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 1), executive summary
evidence.passage: Although human-based modelling can suffer from similar weaknesses of AI models – for example bias or errors – a key distinguishing feature of the former is that humans can be held unambiguously accountable.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 2), executive summary, continuing the same paragraph
evidence.passage: This challenge is compounded by a number of factors, including (i) the speed and scale of AI adoption by financial institutions; (ii) technical construct of AI algorithms; and (iii) lack of model explainability.

records.statement: The Basel Committee's newsletter of 16 March 2022 states that AI/ML models may be more difficult to manage than traditional models because they can be more complex, and names the extent to which model outcomes can be understood and explained as an area for continued discussion.
records.qualification: Informational; not supervisory guidance.

evidence.locator: Second paragraph of the main text, beginning 'In its discussions to date'
evidence.passage: In some cases, AI/ML models may be more difficult to manage than traditional models as they can be more complex.

evidence.locator: First of the three areas listed for continuing discussions
evidence.passage: The first area named for continuing discussions is the extent and degree to which the outcomes of models can be understood and explained.

records.statement: The Basel Committee's report 'Digitalisation of finance' of May 2024 states that generative AI models are complex and opaque, which can make their outcomes harder to explain, and that lack of explainability makes it difficult to assess the conceptual soundness of an AI/ML approach.
records.qualification: Describes model-risk concerns; it also reports that some banks use ML models with 'a good balance between accuracy and explainability' (PDF p. 11).

evidence.locator: PDF p. 26 (printed p. 22), Box 8 'Generative AI risks', bullet 'Explainability'
evidence.passage: these models are complex and opaque, relying on hundreds of billions of parameters which can make it more difficult to explain the model's outcomes.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 22 (printed p. 18), footnote 36
evidence.passage: A key concern with lack of explainability is the difficulty in assessing the conceptual soundness of an AI/ML approach

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2019 (chapter III) states in an endnote that complex and opaque algorithms render biases in machine-learning credit scoring particularly difficult to detect and therefore to prevent.
records.missing: Does not say whose task (firms' risk management or supervisors' assessment) the opacity makes harder; the passage concerns detecting discriminatory bias in big tech algorithms.
records.qualification: An endnote to a chapter on big tech in finance.

evidence.locator: Endnote 16
evidence.passage: The complex and opaque algorithms render biases particularly difficult to detect, and therefore to prevent.

records.statement: In his overview of IFC Bulletin No 44 (September 2017), Bruno Tissot of the BIS reports a Central Bank of Aruba presentation as finding that machine learning models can incorporate seasonal patterns, non-linearities and lagged effects without ex ante assumptions and appear efficient in predictive capacity for nowcasting tourism data.
records.qualification: A relay: the overview summarises a presentation by Central Bank of Aruba staff; the same passage notes the 'limited interpretability' of 'black box' calculations. Staff voice under the overview's disclaimer.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 11, overview section 3, paragraph beginning 'A presentation by the Central Bank of Aruba'
evidence.passage: big data algorithms such as machine learning models allow a wide range of effects to be incorporated (for instance, seasonal patterns, non-linearities, lagged effects) without the need to make ex ante assumptions. Third, these new techniques appear efficient in terms of predictive capacity

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2024 (chapter III) states that large language models and generative AI hold promise for nowcasting by turning unstructured data into structured series, and that sentiment indices derived from such data can substantially improve forecasts of unemployment, GDP growth and inflation.
records.qualification: 'Most developed' is an editorial judgement among this group's located texts (a full box on nowcasting). The chapter also states limits on AI in macroprudential use given scarce crisis data.

evidence.locator: Section 'Harnessing AI for policy objectives', paragraph beginning 'These capabilities are particularly promising for nowcasting'
evidence.passage: LLMs and gen AI hold promise to overcome both bottlenecks (see Box D).

evidence.locator: Box D, paragraph beginning 'Nowcasting models could benefit from deep neural networks' embeddings'
evidence.passage: Such sentiment indices can substantially improve forecasts for key macroeconomic quantities, such as unemployment, GDP growth and inflation.

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2024 (chapter III) states that AI will affect productivity, consumption, investment and labour markets, which have direct effects on price and financial stability, and that these developments are of paramount concern to central banks.
records.qualification: States relevance for central bank mandates; the chapter's section on macroeconomic effects presents scenarios in which AI's initial effect on inflation could be disinflationary or inflationary.

evidence.locator: Section 'Introduction', paragraph beginning 'First, AI will influence central banks' core activities'
evidence.passage: AI will affect financial systems as well as productivity, consumption, investment and labour markets, which themselves have direct effects on price and financial stability.

evidence.locator: Same paragraph, last sentence
evidence.passage: These developments are therefore of paramount concern to central banks.

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2026 (chapter I) states that the AI boom poses several challenges for monetary policy, that AI's longer-term effects on productivity, labour markets and the role of monetary policy remain highly uncertain, and that monetary policy strategies should be robust across a wide range of scenarios.
records.qualification: States policy implications under uncertainty; it prescribes robustness, not a specific response to AI.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 40 (printed p. 30), chapter I, section 'Policy implications', subsection 'Monetary policy'
evidence.passage: The ongoing AI boom also poses several challenges for monetary policy.

evidence.locator: Same paragraph, closing sentences

records.statement: In a speech of 10 September 2026, Pablo Hernández de Cos, General Manager of the BIS, said that AI is making the economy harder to read, increasing uncertainty around the transmission of monetary policy, and can widen errors in estimating potential output and the natural rate of interest.

evidence.locator: Same paragraph, last sentence
evidence.passage: Structural change driven by AI can widen measurement errors, and discrepancies between actual and estimated output gaps may grow.

records.statement: BIS Working Paper No 1194 of June 2024, by Aldasoro, Gambacorta, Korinek, Shreeti and Stein, lists, in its table of the impact of successive AI technologies, faster payment flows and fraud prevention as opportunities of AI agents in payments.
records.missing: A table entry only; does not state that AI agents would initiate, negotiate or execute payments for people or firms.
records.qualification: A staff working paper under the series disclaimer.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 14, Table 1, row 'Payments', column 'AI Agents', opportunities
evidence.passage: Faster payment flows, fraud prevention

crossFamily.result: held for the maintainer under the override rule (earliest-located role). The checker reads this paper as U07’s earliest located text; the preparer reads bears on. The record stays context and BIS Working Paper 1310 keeps the role until the maintainer decides.

readings.checker: articulates, qualified, at whole-document level: Table 1 (PDF p. 14) puts “faster payment flows” under the opportunities of AI agents in payments, and the text (PDF pp. 15–16) says that AI agents “could soon autonomously design, market, and sell financial products and services”; together these meet the transactions limb. records.statement: BIS Working Paper No 1310 of November 2025, by Iñaki Aldasoro and Ajit Desai, reports experiments in which a generative AI agent performed intraday liquidity management in a simulated wholesale payment system, and writes that routine cash-management tasks could be automated using general-purpose large language models.

time.note: Date printed on the title page (the cover gives November 2025): the date of the wording, used for the headline. The BIS page gives “Date Published 26 November 2025” (source bis-wp-1310-page); 10 November is not a verified release day.

records.qualification: A staff working paper under the series disclaimer, based on prompt-based simulations; the agent issued recommendations and deferred to human oversight in anomalous scenarios. It does not show agents executing live payments, and concerns banks' payment operations, not consumer commerce.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 3, abstract
evidence.passage: we evaluate whether a generative artificial intelligence (AI) agent can perform high-level intraday liquidity management in a wholesale payment system.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 3, abstract

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2025 (chapter III) states that, in next-generation correspondent banking on a tokenised platform, further efficiency can be achieved by embedding pre-screening checks into the payment instruction and compliance reporting capabilities through AI agents.

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2026 (chapter III) states that new tools harnessing artificial intelligence and the public ledger of transactions can provide solutions to the financial integrity challenges of stablecoins on public permissionless blockchains, but that those challenges remain substantial.
records.missing: Concerns AI as an integrity tool for stablecoins, not transactions initiated by AI agents or AI's effect on the monetary system.
records.qualification: One sentence in a chapter on stablecoins and tokenisation.

records.statement: The Basel Committee's 'Sound Practices' report of February 2018 states that technologies such as AI/ML and advanced data analytics may also have the potential to improve supervisory efficiency and effectiveness, and that supervisors exploring such technologies could enhance safety and soundness; it uses the term 'suptech'.
records.qualification: Not earliest located in the pack; the report itself cites earlier texts. It describes supervisors' involvement with suptech as nascent and names lack of transparency of AI as a barrier.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 36 (printed p. 35), section C 'Suptech opportunities', Implication 8
evidence.passage: The same technologies that offer efficiencies and opportunities for fintech firms and banks, such as AI/ML/advanced data analytics, DLT, cloud computing and APIs, may also have the potential to improve supervisory efficiency and effectiveness.

evidence.locator: Same page, Consideration 8
evidence.passage: Safety and soundness and financial stability could be enhanced by supervisors investigating and exploring the potential of new technologies to improve their methods and processes

records.statement: FSI Insights No 9 of July 2018, by Dirk Broeders and Jermy Prenio, states that suptech applications, particularly in data analytics, are seen as capable of turning risk and compliance monitoring into a predictive and proactive process, and reports AI/ML applications at supervisory agencies, among them an anti-money-laundering network analysis at the Monetary Authority of Singapore.
records.qualification: A staff paper under the FSI series disclaimer, based on interviews with supervisory agencies; it reports expected benefits and names lack of transparency in some analytics applications as a critical issue.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 1), executive summary
evidence.passage: Suptech applications, particularly in the area of data analytics, are seen as capable of turning risk and compliance monitoring from a backward-looking into a predictive and proactive process.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 14, Box 3 'Natural language processing and machine learning at the Monetary Authority of Singapore'
evidence.passage: Using artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML) to do the same thing will require only a few minutes.
evidence.note: The box relays the Monetary Authority of Singapore's description of its application.

records.statement: In a column of 3 June 2019, Agustín Carstens, General Manager of the BIS, wrote that authorities are harnessing advances in artificial intelligence to help shape new supervisory tools.
records.qualification: The writer's column, published on the BIS site as a management speech; not stated to be a BIS position. A descriptive sentence within a broader text on innovation.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning 'The new waters that central banks are navigating'
evidence.passage: Authorities are harnessing advances in artificial intelligence and its practical applications to help shape new supervisory tools.

records.statement: The Basel Committee's 'Sound Practices' report of February 2018 states that analytics of big data associated with machine learning and AI can support banks' financial crime divisions in monitoring and reporting suspicious transactions.
records.qualification: Concerns AML/CFT; the same report states that the accuracy of AI/ML credit models is unproven (recorded separately as contesting).

evidence.locator: PDF p. 30 (printed p. 29), section on AML/CFT, paragraph on regtech solutions
evidence.passage: Analytics of non-structured data (big data) associated with machine learning and AI can support banks' financial crime divisions in the monitoring and reporting of suspicious transactions.

records.statement: The Basel Committee's 'Sound Practices' report of February 2018 states that the accuracy and validity of AI/ML models increasingly used for the termination of credit limits is as yet unproven.
records.missing: A statement that AI or machine-learning models do not, or cannot, improve risk management; the passage calls their accuracy and validity for the termination of credit limits unproven.
records.qualification: A limited dissent: it calls the models unproven, not inferior, and the same report articulates U10 for AML.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 31 (printed p. 30), subsection 'Artificial intelligence/machine learning/advanced data analytics'
evidence.passage: There is an increasing use of AI/ML for the termination of credit limits, although the accuracy and validity of these models is as yet unproven.

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2019 (chapter III) states that an internal rating system based on machine learning and platform data can outperform simple models based on bureau scores in predicting defaults, while it is an open question whether it outperforms bank models and holds over full cycles.
records.qualification: Based on one case (Mercado Libre) in Box III.B; the chapter states the open question in the same paragraph.

evidence.locator: Box III.B 'Big tech credit assessment: big data and artificial intelligence', paragraph beginning 'Further, the internal rating system'
evidence.passage: the internal rating system based on machine learning techniques and data obtained from the e-commerce platform can outperform simple models based on bureau score and borrower characteristics in predicting defaults

evidence.locator: Same paragraph
evidence.passage: there are open questions as to whether this performance is superior to bank models that use also soft information and can be sustained over full business and financial cycles.

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2025 (chapter III) states that machine learning tools present opportunities to help combat financial crime, reducing false positives and increasing detection of fraudulent transactions.
records.qualification: Concerns AML/CFT compliance; Box B also describes AI agents as possible co-pilots in preparing suspicious activity reports.

evidence.locator: Section 'Stablecoins and the integrity imperative', paragraph beginning 'Technological improvements can enhance the integrity'
evidence.passage: AI and data integration advances, particularly through the development of machine learning tools, present opportunities to help combat financial crime. These innovations help reduce false positives (ie legitimate transactions flagged as illicit) and increase detection of fraudulent transactions.

records.statement: BIS Working Paper No 930 of March 2021, by Sebastian Doerr, Leonardo Gambacorta and Jose Maria Serena, reports that several central banks face constraints in IT infrastructure and human capital for big data and machine learning, and states that cooperation among public authorities could improve central banks' ability to collect, store and analyse big data.
records.qualification: A staff working paper under its disclaimer, drawing on an IFC survey. Its subject is big data used with machine learning, not AI generally.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 3, abstract
evidence.passage: Several institutions report constraints in setting up an adequate IT infrastructure and in developing the necessary human capital. Cooperation among public authorities could improve central banks' ability to collect, store and analyse big data.

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2024 (chapter III) states that central banks need to build expertise in AI, that providing computing power and staff involves high up-front costs, and that central banks need to form a 'community of practice' to share knowledge, data, best practices and AI tools.
records.qualification: It recommends cooperation; it does not report an agreed programme.

evidence.locator: Section 'Introduction', paragraph beginning 'Overall, the rapid and widespread adoption of AI'
evidence.passage: Central banks need to come together to form a "community of practice" to share knowledge, data, best practices and AI tools.

evidence.locator: Section 'Toward an action plan for central banks', paragraph beginning 'The decision on whether to use external or internal models'
evidence.passage: Providing adequate computing power and software, as well as training existing or hiring new staff, involves high up-front costs.

records.statement: In remarks prepared for delivery on 20 October 2026, Tao Zhang, BIS Chief Representative for Asia and the Pacific, said that authorities differ in access to data, technology and expertise for AI, and that international cooperation can narrow these gaps through training, technical assistance and knowledge sharing.
records.qualification: The speaker's own views under his disclaimer, not a BIS position.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning 'There is also an important capacity-building dimension'
evidence.passage: Not every authority has the same access to data, technology or specialised expertise. International cooperation can help to narrow these gaps through training, technical assistance and the sharing of knowledge and practical experience.

records.statement: FSI Insights No 35 of August 2021, by Jermy Prenio and Jeffery Yong, states that existing requirements on governance, risk management and traditional models also apply to AI models, and that most issues arising from AI use are similar to those for traditional models.
records.qualification: A staff paper under the FSI series disclaimer. The same summary also states that there is scope for standard-setting bodies to develop international guidance on AI and calls for a proportional regulatory response.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 1), executive summary
evidence.passage: Existing requirements on governance, risk management, as well as development and operation of traditional models also apply to AI models.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 1), executive summary
evidence.passage: While most of the issues arising from the use of AI by financial institutions are similar to those for traditional models, the perspective might be different.

records.statement: FSI Insights No 63 of December 2024, by Crisanto, Leuterio, Prenio and Yong, states that the common themes of AI guidance are broadly contained in financial regulations on governance, risk management and consumer protection, which may be why most financial authorities have not issued separate AI regulations for financial institutions.
records.qualification: A staff paper under the FSI series disclaimer; the same summary says that guidance may be needed in specific areas (see the context record am-u12-fsi-2024-insights-63-context).

evidence.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 1), executive summary
evidence.passage: The common themes in policy expectations are broadly contained in financial regulations covering governance, risk management and consumer protection. This may be the reason why most financial authorities have not issued separate regulations on AI use by financial institutions.

crossFamily.result: qualification updated: the companion record is now context, not contesting.

records.statement: FSI Insights No 63 of December 2024, by Crisanto, Leuterio, Prenio and Yong, also states that AI use may present unique challenges so that regulatory or supervisory guidance may be needed in specific areas, and that provider concentration strengthens the argument for direct oversight frameworks for cloud and AI service providers.
records.missing: The passages say that guidance may be needed in specific areas and that provider concentration strengthens the case for direct oversight of cloud and AI service providers; they do not dispute that existing rules broadly cover financial institutions’ use of AI, and the same summary states that they do (see the articulating record).

evidence.passage: Nevertheless, AI use by financial institutions may present some unique challenges and hence regulatory or supervisory guidance may be needed in specific areas.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 2), executive summary, bullet 'Regulatory perimeter – third parties'
evidence.passage: The concentration of cloud and AI service providers to a few large global technology firms strengthens the argument for putting in place direct oversight frameworks for these service providers depending on available legal authority.

records.statement: The Basel Committee's report 'Digitalisation of finance' of May 2024 states that some supervisors have clarified that existing requirements on operational, technology, model, IT/cyber and outsourcing risk apply to AI, and that a few jurisdictions have issued specific AI/ML principles or guidance.
records.missing: Reports other supervisors' clarifications; the Committee does not itself state that AI needs no separate framework. Elsewhere (PDF p. 39) it describes a precautionary approach including developing new standards where existing policy is inadequate.

events.subject: Project Aurora, phase 1
events.statement: The BIS Innovation Hub's Project Aurora page states that the Nordic Centre concluded phase 1 of Project Aurora in 2023, a proof of concept applying artificial intelligence, machine learning, privacy-enhancing technologies and network analysis to combating money laundering.

time.note: The page's 'Last updated' date; the event's own date is in eventDate.

events.qualification: States conclusion of a proof of concept on simulated data; the detection figures on the page are the project's own.

evidence.locator: Project page, paragraph beginning 'In 2023, BIS Innovation Hub (Nordic Centre)'
evidence.passage: In 2023, BIS Innovation Hub (Nordic Centre) successfully concluded phase 1 of Project Aurora, a proof of concept that explored new ways of combating money laundering taking a data driven approach, by applying artificial intelligence, machine learning privacy enhancing technologies and network analysis.

events.subject: Project Aurora, new phase
events.statement: The BIS Innovation Hub's Project Aurora page states that the Nordic Centre is launching a new phase of Project Aurora building on phase 1.
events.qualification: Announced stays announced: the page describes a launch in progress and planned aims.

evidence.locator: Project page, opening paragraph
evidence.passage: The BIS Innovation Hub Nordic Centre is launching a new phase of Project Aurora, building on the findings of phase 1, which concluded in 2023.

events.subject: Project Raven
events.statement: The BIS Innovation Hub's Project Raven page states that Project Raven was launched by the Nordic Centre to create a solution using artificial intelligence to help authorities assess the cyber security and resilience of their financial systems.
events.qualification: The page states the launch and the project's aims; it gives no launch date and does not state that the solution is in use.

evidence.locator: Project page, second paragraph
evidence.passage: Project Raven, launched by the BIS Innovation Hub Nordic Centre, aims to create a new solution to help authorities comprehensively assess the cyber security and resilience maturity readiness of their countries' financial systems.

events.subject: Project Gaia proof of concept
events.statement: The BIS Innovation Hub's Project Gaia page states that Gaia, using large language models, delivered a proof of concept that automates identifying climate-related indicators across a large set of corporate reports.
events.qualification: A proof of concept with the Deutsche Bundesbank and the ECB; the page also describes a second phase without stating its completion.

evidence.locator: Project page, paragraph beginning 'The experiment was coordinated by the BIS Innovation Hub Eurosystem Centre'
evidence.passage: Gaia delivered a proof of concept demonstrating it is possible to automate the task of identifying such indicators across a large set of reports

events.subject: Project Spectrum
events.statement: The BIS Innovation Hub's Project Spectrum page states that Project Spectrum, a collaboration of the BIS, the Deutsche Bundesbank and the ECB, explored using AI text embeddings to classify web-scraped product prices for inflation nowcasting.
events.qualification: States work done in an exploratory project (status 'Ongoing'); the cost and accuracy figures on the page are the project's own.

evidence.locator: Project page, paragraph beginning 'Project Spectrum – a collaboration'
evidence.passage: Project Spectrum – a collaboration between the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the Deutsche Bundesbank and the European Central Bank – explored an alternative approach where Artificial intelligence (AI) was used only to transform product descriptions into high-dimensional text embeddings.

events.subject: Project AISE (AI Supervisory Enablement)
events.statement: The BIS Innovation Hub's Project AISE page states that AISE is a technical proof of concept exploring how central banks and supervisory authorities could use AI responsibly in supervisory analytics.
events.qualification: The page states that the project exists and is ongoing (Toronto Centre), using synthetic data; it gives no start date and reports no findings.

evidence.locator: Project page, opening paragraph
evidence.passage: It is a technical proof of concept exploring how central banks and supervisory authorities could use artificial intelligence (AI) responsibly in supervisory analytics.

events.subject: BIS Innovation Hub projects employing AI methods
events.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2024 (chapter III, Box C) states that eight BIS Innovation Hub projects – Ellipse, Aurora, Gaia, Symbiosis, Raven, Neo, Spectrum and Insight – had employed AI methods.
events.qualification: A count as of the report's date; it does not state that any project's tool is in operational use.

evidence.locator: Box C, first paragraph
evidence.passage: So far, eight projects – Ellipse, Aurora, Gaia, Symbiosis, Raven, Neo, Spectrum and Insight – have employed AI methods.

events.subject: Continued analysis of banks' use of AI/ML
events.statement: The Basel Committee's newsletter of 16 March 2022 states that the Committee intends to continue exploring banks' use of AI/ML, focusing on explainability, governance, and resilience and financial stability.
events.qualification: Announced stays announced; the newsletter states an intention and is not guidance.

evidence.locator: Summary paragraphs at the head of the newsletter
evidence.passage: The Committee states that it intends to continue exploring banks' use of AI/ML, especially in the areas of explainability, governance, and resilience and financial stability.
